notes.meaning: Jonathan had been busy chasing the enemy and never heard his father place the army under a curse. When he saw wild honey dripping in the woods, he dipped the end of his staff into it and ate a little. The food instantly gave him fresh energy, making his eyes bright after being worn out and hungry.

A soldier told Jonathan about the strict oath Saul had placed on the whole army. Saul had declared anyone cursed who ate any food that day, which left the men dizzy and weak from hunger. The warning explained why the soldiers were exhausted instead of celebrating their success.

Jonathan openly stated that his father had brought trouble on the nation with such a foolish rule. He pointed to his own renewed strength from just a taste of honey to prove how much food helps in battle. If the soldiers had been allowed to eat from the captured supplies, they could have won a far greater victory over the Philistines.

The Israelite soldiers pursued and fought the Philistines across many miles from Michmash to Aijalon. By the end of this long chase, the troops were completely drained of energy. Their extreme weariness set the stage for bad decisions as soon as the day ended.

Once evening came and Saul's fast was over, the starving men pounced wildly on the captured farm animals. They butchered sheep and cattle right on the dirt and ate the meat before the blood could drain out. In their desperate hunger, they broke God's direct law against eating meat with blood still in it.

When Saul learned that the army was breaking God's law by eating meat with blood, he rebuked the men for being unfaithful. He commanded them to roll a large stone over to him at once. This rock was meant to serve as an elevated surface so the blood could drain out properly onto the ground.

Saul sent messengers through the camp ordering each soldier to bring his animal to the stone for proper slaughter. The men obeyed and brought their cattle that night so they could eat without sinning against the Lord. Saul was quick to correct the people's ritual mistake, though he failed to see that his own rash vow had caused their desperation.

Saul built an altar to the Lord, which was the very first altar he had ever built. It may have served to offer sacrifices of thanksgiving for the victory or to ask forgiveness for the people's sin. It showed that Saul kept up outward religious duties even while his heart was drifting from true obedience.

After the troops ate, Saul wanted to pursue the Philistines all night long and wipe them out completely before dawn. The weary soldiers simply agreed to whatever the king wanted to do. Ahijah the priest wisely stepped in, insisting that they stop and ask God for guidance before rushing into another fight.

Saul asked God whether Israel should attack the Philistines by night and whether He would hand them over. God gave no answer at all through the sacred priestly stones. The Lord's silence was a clear warning that something was wrong in the camp.

Saul called all the leaders together to find out what sin had caused God to go silent. He rashly swore by the living God that whoever was guilty would be put to death, even if it turned out to be his own son Jonathan. The soldiers knew Jonathan had eaten honey, but out of love and loyalty to him, not one person said a word.

Saul organized a formal lot to locate the offender, placing all the troops on one side and himself and Jonathan on the other. The people offered no resistance and told the king to do whatever he thought best. Saul was confident that the guilt lay somewhere else rather than with his own rash leadership.

Saul prayed and asked the God of Israel to reveal the truth through the sacred lots. The lot cleared the army and pointed directly to Saul and Jonathan. God allowed the lot to expose the situation so Saul's foolish oath would be brought into the open.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars prefer the longer reading found in the ancient Greek Septuagint, which describes Saul specifically asking God to answer by the priestly lots of Urim and Thummim to decide between the royal family and the army.

notes.meaning: Saul ordered the lot cast between just the two of them, and it fell on Jonathan. God did not single out Jonathan because eating the honey was an evil act, but to reveal who had technically breached the king's vow. The result forced Saul to face the harsh consequence of his own words.

Saul commanded his son to tell him what he had done. Jonathan plainly admitted that he had only tasted a little honey on the tip of his staff, and he expressed grief that he was now expected to die for such a harmless act. He did not lie or make excuses, facing the outcome with quiet courage.

Saul pronounced a death sentence on Jonathan, invoking a curse on himself if he failed to carry it out. He placed the literal keeping of his own foolish oath above mercy and common sense. In his stubborn pride, he was willing to kill his most heroic son rather than admit his command had been wrong.

differ.view: Saul acted out of a genuine fear of God and deserves credit for putting his religious oath above his personal feelings for his son.
Saul acted out of pride, fury, and a cruel misunderstanding of duty, much like Jephthah making a tragic and unlawful vow.

notes.meaning: The army firmly stood up to Saul and refused to let Jonathan die. They pointed out that God had worked through Jonathan that day to win a great deliverance for Israel, and they swore that not a single hair of his head would fall. The soldiers overruled the king and saved Jonathan's life.

Saul stopped chasing the Philistines, and they were able to retreat safely to their own territory. Because of the delay, confusion, and division caused by Saul's oath, an opportunity for total victory was lost. When a leader causes strife among God's people, the work of God suffers.

Once Saul had firmly established his royal rule, he fought against enemies on every border, including Moab, Ammon, Edom, Zobah, and the Philistines. He also fought bravely against the Amalekites and protected Israel from invaders who raided their land. God gave Saul natural military ability to defend the nation, even though his reign was full of trouble.

These verses record the key members of Saul's household and leadership. He had three sons named Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua, and two daughters named Merab and Michal. His wife was Ahinoam, and his top army commander was his cousin Abner, uniting the royal family with military command.

Saul had to fight hard battles against the Philistines throughout his entire lifetime. To keep up the fight, he personally drafted every brave and strong young man he saw into his standing army. While he built up human military power, his reign continued to lack the full peace that only God's blessing can give.
